title: The internet runs on cats: what the research actually says
description: Cats are the internet's unofficial mascot, and the programmer's desk cat is a stereotype. But is there evidence that tech people prefer cats? Along the way: the neural network that learned "cat" without being told what one was, a survey of nearly 7,000 people about why they watch cat videos, an Ig Nobel prize for asking whether cats are liquid, and software that locks your keyboard when a cat walks on it. Every Question separates a fun claim from what the evidence supports.
author: Quizbun

questions.title: Is there solid evidence that people in IT like cats more than other people do?

options.text: No. The largest developer survey we found leaned toward dogs, and it had no non-developers to compare with
Yes. Stack Overflow's developer survey shows it every year
Yes. A 2014 personality study of programmers proved it
No. Studies show IT people are allergic to cats more often

questions.explanation:
Stack Overflow asked "Dogs or cats?" in its 2016 Developer Survey. Of the 45,239 respondents who answered, 48.9% picked dogs, 34.8% cats and 16.4% something else. Germany was the exception, with cats ahead of dogs.

Even that survey can't settle the question as asked. "More than other people" is a comparison, and nobody outside software answered the same question in the same survey. A dog-leaning result among developers is compatible with developers being *more* cat-friendly than the general public, *less*, or the same. We found no large study that compares pet preference across occupations. That is weaker than "no such study exists", so read it as "not shown" rather than "disproved".

Evidence for the stereotype: none that we could find. It's a cultural joke.
questions.references: [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2016: overview](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2016/), [Stack Overflow 2016 raw results (CSV, column `dogs_vs_cats`)](https://github.com/StackExchange/Survey/tree/main/packages/archive/2016)

images.alt: Bar chart of the 2016 Stack Overflow survey question "Dogs or cats?". All 45,239 respondents: dogs 48.9%, cats 34.8%, other 16.4%. Germany, 3,154 respondents: dogs 38.4%, cats 44.5%, other 17.0%. A note says only developers answered, so the chart cannot compare developers with anyone else.
images.caption: Percentages computed from Stack Overflow's published 2016 raw data, counting only people who answered the question. Chart drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: What kind of study could actually show whether IT workers prefer cats more than other people do?

options.text: A representative survey of many occupations that asks everyone the same pet question, then compares IT workers with the rest
A poll on a programming forum asking members whether they like cats
Counting cat photos in developers' social media posts
Interviewing a dozen well-known programmers about their pets

questions.explanation:
The claim compares two groups, so the study needs both groups, measured the same way.

- **A comparison group.** A forum poll only reaches programmers. Even a perfect result tells you what programmers like, not whether they like it *more*.
- **Representative sampling.** People who answer a cat poll on a forum, or post cat photos, choose themselves. People who love cats are more likely to take part, which inflates the result.
- **The same measure for everyone.** Counting photos measures posting habits, and cats may simply be easier to photograph at a desk than dogs.

Famous programmers are a handful of memorable cases, which is how stereotypes form in the first place. Anything short of the first design stays anecdote.

questions.title: A 2014 study reported that self-described "cat people" were more introverted than "dog people". Which of these limit what it can tell us about programmers?
questions.description: Psychologist Denise Guastello of Carroll University surveyed about 600 college students on their pet preference and personality.

options.text: The participants were college students, not workers in IT or any other field
Pet preference and personality were both self-reported on questionnaires
It found an association, which can't show whether cats make people introverted, introverts choose cats, or neither
About 600 people is too few for any statistical test to work
Introversion was measured with brain scans, which are known to be unreliable

questions.explanation:
The study asked students whether they considered themselves dog lovers or cat lovers, then gave them personality questionnaires. Dog lovers scored as more energetic and outgoing. Cat lovers scored as more introverted, open-minded and sensitive.

To get from there to "programmers like cats" you need two leaps the data doesn't support. First, students aren't programmers, and nothing in the study measured occupation. Second, even if programmers were more introverted on average, a link between introversion and cats in students doesn't carry over to a different population automatically.

The sample size isn't the problem. Six hundred people is plenty to detect a moderate difference between groups. The problems are *who* was sampled and *what kind* of evidence it is: self-reported and correlational, with no brain scans or behavior observed.

Evidence that cat people are more introverted: one correlational survey of students.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Cat people and dog people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_people_and_dog_people), [CBS News: "Dog people" and "cat people" have different personality traits (2014)](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/dog-people-and-cat-people-have-different-personality-traits-study-finds/), [Wikipedia: Correlation does not imply causation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correlation_does_not_imply_causation)

questions.title: In 2012, a Google network learned to detect cats from YouTube stills. How many of its training images were labeled "cat"?

options.text: None
About 10,000
About half of them
All of them, because it was only shown cats

questions.explanation:
Not one. The training set was 10 million frames, one from each of 10 million YouTube videos, with no labels of any kind. This is **unsupervised learning**.

The network was a sparse autoencoder. Its only goal was to rebuild each input image after squeezing it through layers that could keep just a few active features at a time. To do that well on YouTube frames, it had to find patterns that recur often. Human faces are one, and cat faces turned out to be another. After training, the researchers searched the top layer for neurons that reacted to test images of cats, and one reacted strongly. Nobody had defined "cat"; the concept came from the data.

Labels came later, and only for a different test: recognizing 22,000 ImageNet categories, where labeled examples were used to train a classifier on top of the learned features.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012): Building high-level features using large scale unsupervised learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [Google blog: Using large-scale brain simulations for machine learning and A.I. (2012)](https://blog.google/technology/ai/using-large-scale-brain-simulations-for/), [Wikipedia: Autoencoder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoencoder)

images.alt: Three boxes joined by arrows. First: 10 million frames, one per YouTube video, 200 by 200 pixels, no labels at all. Second: a 9-layer sparse autoencoder with about 1 billion connections, trained on 16,000 cores for 3 days. Third: one top-layer neuron fires strongly for cat faces, with others for human faces and bodies. A note says the training goal was to rebuild each input image from a compressed, sparse code.
images.caption: Figures from Le et al. (2012). Diagram drawn for this Quiz; the paper's own visualization of the cat neuron is linked in References rather than copied.

questions.title: What hardware did Google's 2012 cat-detecting network train on?

options.text: A cluster of 1,000 machines with 16,000 CPU cores, for three days
A single high-end gaming GPU, overnight
Sixteen machines with one GPU each, for a month
A laptop, because the network had only a few thousand connections

questions.explanation:
The model had about 1 billion connections and trained on 10 million 200 × 200 pixel images. That didn't fit on one machine, so the team split the model itself across machines (model parallelism) and ran many copies at once that sent updates to shared parameter servers (asynchronous SGD). The whole job used 1,000 machines and 16,000 CPU cores for three days.

The GPU answers are tempting because GPUs power almost all deep learning today. In 2012 they were only starting to take over. The same year, AlexNet won the ImageNet competition on two GPUs, and that result did much more to change how networks were trained.

The point of the scale was the paper's real question: can you get high-level concepts out of unlabeled data at all, if the model and the dataset are big enough?

questions.title: The cat test set was about 35% cat faces and 65% other images. What accuracy, in percent, does a lazy classifier get by answering "not a cat" every time?
questions.description: The paper's face test had 13,026 positives among 37,000 images, and the cat test used the same ratio. Round to one decimal place.
questions.explanation:
With the face test's counts, 23,974 negatives ÷ 37,000 images ≈ 0.648, so answering "not a cat" for everything scores **64.8%** without looking at a single pixel. The paper lists exactly this as its "random guess" baseline.

That's the frame for the famous cat neuron. Its best accuracy was **74.8%**: about 10 points above doing nothing, and 7.6 points above the best simple linear filter (67.2%). The face neuron did better, at 81.7%, and a human-body neuron reached 76.7%.

The result is real, and it was remarkable in 2012 for a network that had never seen a label. But a headline number means little until you know what the do-nothing baseline scores. Whenever the classes in a test are unbalanced, check that first.

Evidence that the network learned a cat concept: strong, but it's a modest detector, not a reliable one.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012), Section 5 and Table 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [Wikipedia: Accuracy paradox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accuracy_paradox)

images.alt: Bar chart on a 0 to 100 percent axis. Always answering "not a cat": 64.8%. Best simple linear filter: 67.2%. Best cat neuron: 74.8%. A dashed line at 64.8% marks accuracy that needs no learning.
images.caption: Numbers from Table 1 of Le et al. (2012). Chart drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: Besides cat faces, which concepts did the 2012 paper report neurons responding to?

options.text: Human faces
Human bodies
Dogs
Written text

questions.explanation:
The paper is mostly about **faces**. Its opening question was whether you could learn a face detector from unlabeled images, and its best face neuron scored 81.7%. The authors then asked whether other things common on YouTube had also been learned. They built two more test sets, found a **cat-face** neuron (74.8%) and a **human-body** neuron (76.7%), and stopped there.

Dogs and text weren't reported because the authors didn't test for them, which is different from finding they weren't learned. A neuron for dogs may or may not have existed; nobody looked.

The cat became the headline because it's funnier than faces. Ask what a result was *about* before you retell it.
questions.references: [Le et al. (2012), Sections 4 and 5](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [NPR: A massive Google network learns to identify — cats (2012)](https://www.npr.org/2012/06/26/155792609/a-massive-google-network-learns-to-identify)

questions.title: In 2015, media researcher Jessica Myrick surveyed nearly 7,000 people about watching cat videos online. How did the survey reach them?

options.text: Mostly through social media, helped by the owner of Lil Bub, a celebrity internet cat
A random telephone sample of U.S. households
Students in an introductory psychology course
Volunteers randomly assigned to watch cat or dog videos in a lab

questions.explanation:
Lil Bub's owner, Mike Bridavsky, helped spread the survey on social media, and 6,795 people answered. That produced a large sample quickly. It is also a sample of people who follow a famous cat online.

This matters for everything the survey found next. A large sample shrinks random error, but it doesn't fix **selection bias**: 7,000 cat fans can tell you a lot about cat fans and much less about everyone else. Only the lab option would test cause and effect, because random assignment is what separates "cat videos change mood" from "people in a certain mood seek out cat videos". This study didn't do that.

Myrick's study is a published, useful survey. Just keep its sample in mind for the next three Questions.
questions.references: [Myrick (2015), Computers in Human Behavior 52: Emotion regulation, procrastination, and watching cat videos online](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2015.06.001), [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Selection bias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selection_bias)

questions.title: What did respondents in Myrick's survey report about how they felt after watching cat videos?

options.text: More energetic
More positive
Less anxious, annoyed and sad
Measurably more productive at work afterward
A lower heart rate

questions.explanation:
Respondents said they felt more energetic and more positive after watching cat videos than before, and reported fewer negative emotions such as anxiety, annoyance and sadness.

The key word is *reported*. These were answers to a one-time online survey, not measurements. Nobody took anyone's pulse, and nobody measured work output. The press release suggests the lift in mood *may* help people take on hard tasks afterward. That is a hypothesis, and the study didn't test it.

A survey like this is a reasonable way to learn how people experience something, and a poor way to learn what it does to them.

Evidence that cat videos lift mood: self-reported, from a self-selected sample of cat fans.
questions.references: [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Self-report study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-report_study)

questions.title: Many respondents watched cat videos at work or while studying. How did they describe the guilt of procrastinating?

options.text: They felt some guilt, but the enjoyment outweighed it
They felt no guilt at all
The guilt outweighed the enjoyment, so they felt worse overall
The survey didn't ask about guilt

questions.explanation:
Guilt was part of the question, because the study was about procrastination and emotion regulation as much as about cats. Respondents did feel guilty about watching when they should have been working or studying. They also said the pleasure outweighed that guilt.

One detail shows how passive most of this viewing was: only about a quarter of the cat videos people watched were ones they had searched for. They came across the rest in feeds and on sites like Facebook, YouTube and BuzzFeed.

If you're reading this at work, you're in good company, according to people who were also reading about cats at work.
questions.references: [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Procrastination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procrastination)

questions.title: According to Myrick's survey, who was more likely to watch cat videos?

options.text: People who own or have owned cats
People who scored higher on agreeableness
People who scored higher on shyness
People who work in IT

questions.explanation:
Cat owners, past and present, watched more, as did respondents who scored higher on agreeableness and shyness. About 36% of respondents called themselves "cat people", and 60% said they liked both cats and dogs.

The IT option is the stereotype sneaking back in. The published summaries of the study don't report anything about occupation, so the survey can't back it either way.

These are associations inside an unusual sample. "Shy people watch more cat videos" is a fair summary of the data. "Cat videos attract shy people" and "cat videos make people shy" are causal stories the design can't separate.
questions.references: [ScienceDaily: Viewing cat videos boosts energy, positive emotions (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Agreeableness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agreeableness)

questions.title: A physicist asked whether cats are liquids. What decides the answer?

options.text: How long you watch: over minutes a cat flows to fill its container, but in a snapshot it keeps its shape
The cat's body temperature
Whether the container is glass or ceramic
Nothing. The paper was a joke with no physics in it

questions.explanation:
Marc-Antoine Fardin, who studies rheology (how materials flow and deform), started from a practical definition: a liquid changes its shape to fit its container. Many photos online show cats doing exactly that in sinks, boxes and jars.

The twist is that "liquid" isn't a fixed property. It depends on the **timescale**. Every material has a *relaxation time*, roughly how long it takes to adapt its shape. Divide that by how long you observe and you get the **Deborah number**, *De*. Below 1, the material flows during your observation and behaves as a liquid. Above 1, it keeps its shape and behaves as a solid. Glaciers flow over years. Silly Putty bounces when thrown but slumps into a puddle over hours.

A cat that settles into a sink over a few minutes is liquid on that timescale. The same cat in a 1/100 s photo is solid.

The last Option is the one to unlearn. Fardin's paper, *On the rheology of cats* (Rheology Bulletin, 2014), is playful but uses real rheology, and it won the **2017 Ig Nobel Prize in Physics**.

Evidence that cats are liquid: depends on how long you watch, which is the point.
questions.references: [Fardin in The Conversation: Answering the question that won me the Ig Nobel Prize: are cats liquid?](https://theconversation.com/answering-the-question-that-won-me-the-ig-nobel-prize-are-cats-liquid-86589), [Fardin (2014): On the rheology of cats, annotated at Fermat's Library](https://fermatslibrary.com/s/on-the-rheology-of-cats), [Wikipedia: Deborah number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_number)

images.alt: A tabby-and-white cat asleep in a bathroom sink, curled so tightly that its body follows the round curve of the basin.
images.caption: Photo by Anagoria, [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:20190410_230530_Cat_Lissy_in_Bathroom_Sink_anagoria.jpg).

images.alt: A logarithmic scale of the Deborah number from 0.001 to 10,000, split at 1. Left of 1 is labeled "it flows (liquid)", right of 1 "it keeps its shape (solid)". A cat napping in a sink for an hour sits at about 0.017, on the liquid side. A cat in a 1/100 second photo sits at 6,000, on the solid side. A note says the example assumes a cat takes about 1 minute to settle into its container.
images.caption: De = relaxation time ÷ observation time. The one-minute relaxation time is an assumption for illustration. Diagram drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: Suppose a kitten takes about 1 minute to settle into the shape of a box. If you watch it for 10 seconds, is it a liquid or a solid?
questions.description: Use De = relaxation time ÷ observation time, where De < 1 means it flows and De > 1 means it keeps its shape.

options.text: A solid: De = 60 ÷ 10 = 6, so it can't change shape in time
A liquid: De = 10 ÷ 60 ≈ 0.17, so it flows
A liquid, because kittens are softer than adult cats
Neither: De is exactly 1 for any living animal

questions.explanation:
Relaxation time goes on top: 60 s ÷ 10 s = **6**. That's greater than 1, so in a 10-second look the kitten doesn't have time to adapt its shape. On that timescale, it's a solid.

The tempting wrong answer flips the fraction. Both numbers are in seconds, so the units don't catch the mistake. Remember it by the extremes: a very long observation should push De toward zero and let everything flow, as with mountains on geological timescales. That only works if observation time is on the bottom.

Watch the same kitten for an hour and De = 60 ÷ 3,600 ≈ 0.017: liquid. The kitten hasn't changed. The only thing that changed is how long you watched.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Deborah number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_number), [Fardin in The Conversation: are cats liquid?](https://theconversation.com/answering-the-question-that-won-me-the-ig-nobel-prize-are-cats-liquid-86589)

images.caption: Photo by Catboy69, [CC0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/), via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_in_a_box_3.jpg).

questions.title: PawSense is software that notices when a cat walks across your keyboard. How does it tell a cat from a person?

options.text: It analyzes which keys are pressed together and the timing between presses
It watches through the webcam for fur
It detects body heat through the keys
It listens through the microphone for purring

questions.explanation:
PawSense uses the only data a keyboard gives it: which keys went down, in what combinations, and when. People type one key at a time, mostly in word-like bursts. A paw presses a clump of neighboring keys almost at once, with a rhythm no typist produces. Its maker says it usually spots a cat within one or two pawsteps.

Then it does two things. It blocks the cat's input, so random keypresses don't reach your programs, and it plays a sound that annoys cats, so they learn to stay off the keyboard even when no one is there.

This is classification from behavior: no camera or special hardware, just patterns in ordinary input. Fraud detection and bot detection often work the same way, using typing rhythm and click timing.

images.alt: Two keyboards side by side. On the left, a person typing "cat" presses C, then A, then T, one key at a time and far apart; the timeline below shows three evenly spaced key-down events. On the right, a paw presses six neighboring keys, D, F, G, C, V and B, at almost the same moment; its timeline shows a tight burst of events.
images.caption: An illustration of the kind of signal PawSense reads, not its actual algorithm. Drawn for this Quiz.

questions.title: PawSense won the Ig Nobel Prize in Computer Science in 2000. What are the Ig Nobel Prizes for?

options.text: Achievements that first make people laugh, and then make them think
Mocking research that is useless or fraudulent
Research that failed peer review but deserved a second look
The funniest papers, as chosen by the Nobel Foundation

questions.explanation:
The Ig Nobels "honor achievements that first make people laugh, and then make them think". The *Annals of Improbable Research* has run them since 1991, and they have no connection to the Nobel Foundation.

Most winners are real, published work with an odd or funny angle. Chris Niswander won for PawSense in 2000. Marc-Antoine Fardin's rheology of cats won Physics in 2017. The laugh comes from the question, and the thinking comes from taking it seriously: timescales in materials, classification from input patterns.

The mocking distractor has a grain of truth. A few prizes have been awarded ironically as criticism. That's the exception, and neither cat prize is one of them.
questions.references: [Wikipedia: Ig Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ig_Nobel_Prize), [Wikipedia: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ig_Nobel_Prize_winners)

questions.title: The Unix `cat` command isn't named after the animal. Type the word it is short for.
questions.explanation:
The manual page says it outright: `cat - concatenate files and print on the standard output`. *Concatenate* means to join things end to end, which is the command's real job:

```bash
cat part1.txt part2.txt > whole.txt
```

Printing a single file with `cat notes.txt` is the special case of concatenating one file onto nothing.

Because `cat` is so familiar, people pipe it into commands that could read the file themselves, as in `cat log.txt | grep error` instead of `grep error log.txt`. Unix folklore calls that a "useless use of cat". It's harmless in a terminal, but it starts an extra process.

Try it now: open a terminal and run `man cat`.

questions.title: GitHub's mascot, the Octocat, began as stock clip art. What had its designer, Simon Oxley, called it?

options.text: Octopuss
Gitty
Kraken Kitty
Tentacat

questions.explanation:
Oxley drew a cat's head with octopus tentacles and sold it on iStock as **Octopuss**, from *octopus* plus *pussycat*. GitHub's founders found it while looking for an image for the site, negotiated exclusive rights with Oxley, and renamed it the Octocat.

It's a useful reminder that stock images come with license terms. Using clip art is one thing; building a brand around it is another, and that took an agreement with the artist.

The Octocat is also one more cat in the "programmers love cats" story. It shows the stereotype is fun and visible, and the earlier Questions showed that visibility isn't evidence.

questions.title: Which of these claims does the evidence in this Quiz support?

options.text: A neural network can learn to detect cat faces better than a do-nothing baseline without ever seeing a labeled cat
In Stack Overflow's 2016 survey, more responding developers picked dogs than cats
Whether a cat behaves as a liquid depends on how long you observe it
Developers like cats more than the general public does
Watching cat videos makes office workers more productive
Owning a cat makes people more introverted

questions.explanation:
The three supported claims each rest on evidence that matches their wording:

- **Cat detector:** a published experiment with a held-out test set. The best cat neuron scored 74.8% against a 64.8% baseline. That's modest but real.
- **Dogs versus cats:** Stack Overflow's own data, 48.9% to 34.8%. The claim stays inside what was measured: developers who answered one survey in 2016.
- **Liquid cats:** the Deborah number follows from the definitions. Watch long enough and the cat flows; watch briefly and it doesn't.

The unsupported claims overreach in a familiar way:

- **Developers versus the public** needs a comparison group that no study we found has.
- **Productivity** was never measured. Myrick's respondents *reported* better mood, and they were cat fans reached through a celebrity cat's followers.
- **Cats cause introversion** turns a correlation in college students into cause and effect.

That's the habit this Quiz is for: before repeating a fun claim, ask what kind of evidence it rests on and whether the claim stays inside it.

(2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.6209), [Stack Overflow Developer Survey 2016](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2016/), [ScienceDaily: Myrick cat video study (2015)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2015/06/150616093357.htm), [Wikipedia: Deborah number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deborah_number)
